title: The future of 3D NAND flash technology
authors: Prasanna Venkatesan, Taeyoung Song, Gaurav Thareja, Luca Larcher, Andrea Padovani, Cristian Zambelli, Shimeng Yu, Suman Datta, Tajana Rosing, Priyankka Ravikumar, Biswajit Ray, Raisul Islam, Wanki Kim, Daewon Ha, Asif Khan
abstract: 3D NAND flash has become the foundational non-volatile storage platform of the AI era, underpinning workloads from model training to large-scale inference and cold data archival. With roadmaps now targeting kilolayer stacks and tens of trillions of devices per die, scaling is no longer governed primarily by process integration or lithography. Instead, it is increasingly constrained by the physics of charge storage itself: lateral charge migration, electrostatic coupling, read disturb, and transport limitations are entering a margin-limited regime. In this regime, their collective interaction, not any single mechanism, compresses operating margins with each generation. In this Perspective, we examine these converging bottlenecks and argue that sustaining NAND scaling will require application-specific co-optimization rather than a monolithic device roadmap. In this framework, conventional charge-trap flash, ferroelectric storage, alternative channel materials, and system-level integration are best viewed as complementary solutions targeted to distinct tiers of data-centric computing.
summary: This perspective paper analyzes the physical limits facing 3D NAND flash memory as it scales to unprecedented heights. It argues that no single technology can sustain future scaling, necessitating a tailored, application-specific co-optimization approach. The paper surveys complementary solutions, including ferroelectric materials and advanced packaging, to meet the diverse demands of AI and data centers.
main_problem: The primary challenge is sustaining the scaling of 3D NAND flash memory beyond current physical limits, which are no longer governed by lithography but by the physics of charge storage itself.
main_result: Sustaining future NAND scaling requires a shift from a monolithic roadmap to an application-specific co-optimization framework, integrating conventional charge-trap flash with complementary technologies like ferroelectric storage.
method: The paper reviews and synthesizes knowledge from various physical bottlenecks (e.g., charge migration, read disturb) and architectural scaling vectors (vertical, lateral, logical, packaging).
model_or_system: The core system is 3D NAND flash, analyzed across its evolution from Charge-Trap Flash (CTF) architectures to advanced concepts like Ferroelectric NAND (FeNAND) and integration with compute units (HBF/CIM).
key_observables: Lateral charge migration, electrostatic coupling, read disturb, string current degradation, and threshold-voltage variability.
important_parameters: Kilolayer stacks (approaching $>20 \mu	ext{m}$), aspect ratios $>60:1$, and the operating regimes of cold vs. active storage.
main_assumptions: The collective interaction of multiple physical bottlenecks compresses operating margins, necessitating co-optimization across different computing tiers.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the four independent scaling vectors (vertical, lateral, logical, architectural) and compare CTF limitations against ferroelectric alternatives within an application-specific co-optimization framework.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the context of 3D NAND's importance, details the physical bottlenecks limiting scaling, argues for the necessity of application-specific co-optimization, and surveys complementary technologies.
why_interesting: While focused on memory, the discussion of charge trapping, state degradation, and the interplay between physical mechanisms (like coupling and variability) mirrors challenges in designing robust quantum memory or superconducting qubits.
